title: PAUL TOLD HUSBANDS TO LOVE THEIR WIVES AS THEIR OWN BODIES — AND THAT CHANGES EVERYTHING
paragraphs: PAUL TOLD HUSBANDS TO LOVE THEIR WIVES AS THEIR OWN BODIES — AND THAT CHANGES EVERYTHING
What if the verse many husbands have read casually is actually a mirror—and what if, when you finally understand what Paul said, you can no longer look at your marriage the same way?
There is a woman somewhere tonight lying beside the man she married...
His wedding ring is still on his hand.
But somehow, somewhere between the vows and the bills, between raising children and surviving disappointments, between unanswered conversations and wounds neither of them knew how to heal...
she began wondering whether she was still cherished.
And somewhere else, there is a husband sitting quietly in his car before walking into his own house.
At least he believes he does.
He has sacrificed things nobody notices.
But something inside their marriage is dying, and he doesn't know how to reach for her anymore.
Maybe he thinks love means paying the bills.
Maybe she thinks his silence means indifference.
Maybe both of them are hurting.
Maybe both of them have become experts at sleeping beside pain.
Then Paul writes words that refuse to leave a husband comfortable:
“οὕτως ὀφείλουσιν καὶ οἱ ἄνδρες ἀγαπᾶν τὰς ἑαυτῶν γυναῖκας ὡς τὰ ἑαυτῶν σώματα...”
Houtōs opheilousin kai hoi andres agapan tas heautōn gynaikas hōs ta heautōn sōmata.
“In the same way husbands ought to love their wives as their own bodies.”
Because Paul is not giving husbands a romantic suggestion.
The Greek verb ὀφείλουσιν — opheilousin carries the sense of ought, of being obligated or indebted.
And the word translated “love” is ἀγαπᾶν — agapan, from agapaō.
Paul is describing a love that is not merely an emotion that survives only while the marriage feels easy.
But there is something even more confronting here.
Paul tells the husband to love his wife ὡς τὰ ἑαυτῶν σώματα — hōs ta heautōn sōmata...
ὁ ἀγαπῶν τὴν ἑαυτοῦ γυναῖκα ἑαυτὸν ἀγαπᾷ
“The one loving his own wife loves himself.”
The question is no longer merely:
“Does the way I treat her look like the way Christ is teaching me to understand love?”
Because Ephesians 5:28 did not fall out of heaven by itself.
Just three verses earlier, Paul gives husbands the terrifyingly beautiful standard:
“Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her.”
The Cross standing in the middle of the marriage.
Not whatever our wounds taught us.
Paul does not tell the husband, “Make sure she deserves your love today.”

That means Christian headship can never honestly be used as permission for selfishness, intimidation, cruelty, humiliation, coercion, manipulation, violence, or treating a wife as spiritually inferior.
The model Paul gives the husband is the crucified Christ.
The One whose strength does not need to crush someone weaker to prove that it is strength.
And suddenly the verse becomes uncomfortable.
we know how quickly we respond when our own bodies hurt.
But what happens when she hurts?
When she says, “I'm tired,” do you hear weakness...
or do you hear the woman who has been carrying things you may never have noticed?
When she tries to tell you something is wrong, do you immediately defend yourself?
Or can you listen long enough to understand the wound before explaining your intention?
When you embarrass her in front of other people, do you dismiss it because you thought it was funny?
When she is emotionally bleeding, do you call her dramatic because you cannot see the wound?
You would not knowingly leave your own hand pressed against a burning stove.
So why would you knowingly leave the woman God joined to you burning in loneliness?
This is where Scripture stops being something we post...
and becomes something that examines us.
Some husbands know every argument necessary to defend biblical marriage...
but have forgotten to kiss their wives goodnight.
Some know how to demand respect...
Some will fight strangers for dishonoring their wives while dishonoring those same wives with their words behind closed doors.
And some men are reading this with tears forming because they already know.
You remember the night she cried.
You remember the apology you never gave.
You remember how affectionate you were when you were trying to win her heart...
and how ordinary you allowed her heart to become once you had it.
do not stop reading at conviction.
Jesus did not die only for respectable sins.
He died for the ugly ones too.
The cold silence designed to punish.
The ego that refuses to say, “I was wrong.”
The heart that wants forgiveness from God while withholding tenderness from the person sleeping beside it.
The Cross is where excuses die...
but it is also where sinners find mercy.
Maybe your marriage has become something neither of you imagined on your wedding day.
Maybe years of unresolved anger built walls so high that you no longer remember how to climb them.
Maybe you are still married legally...
but emotionally you have been living like strangers.
And perhaps the most frightening sentence in your house has become:
And the scandal of grace is that Christ is not frightened by the chapter you are ashamed to admit exists.
Repentance does not mean pretending the damage never happened.
It means bringing sin into God's light.
It means seeking forgiveness without demanding immediate trust.
It means getting help when help is needed.
It means understanding that saying “I'm sorry” is not always the completion of repentance.
Sometimes it is only its first sentence.
A husband shaped by Christ does not say:
“I apologized. Why aren't you over it?”
And sometimes love looks surprisingly ordinary.
Speaking gently when anger would be easier.
Protecting her dignity when she is not in the room.
Holding her while she cries even when you cannot fix what hurts.
this passage is not permission to weaponize Scripture against your husband either.
The Gospel does not hand either spouse ammunition.
Ephesians eventually speaks of the profound mystery of marriage in relation to Christ and the church.
That means Christian marriage was never designed merely to make two people look successful.
And perhaps that is why the enemy delights in destroying marriages.
Because a marriage being transformed by Christ becomes a living testimony that broken things do not have to remain what sin made them.
Biblical teaching about marriage must never be twisted into telling someone experiencing abuse that faithfulness requires silently enduring danger.
Sacrificial love is not the same thing as enabling evil.
Forgiveness does not make violence righteous.
Grace does not require pretending abuse did not occur.
Bringing darkness into the light may include seeking trustworthy pastoral counsel, professional help, legal protection, or immediate safety when necessary.
Jesus does not need us to rename evil “love” in order to defend marriage.
And maybe right now this article is no longer about somebody else's marriage.
I have been physically present and emotionally absent.
I wish he understood how lonely I've been.
Maybe you're divorced and reading this through tears, wondering where these words were ten years ago.
Maybe you're single and suddenly realizing that biblical marriage requires far more than finding somebody attractive.
Maybe you've survived forty years together.
Maybe it is hanging by a thread.
Because ultimately Ephesians 5 is bigger than marriage.
The husband who is commanded to love eventually discovers that he himself survives only because Christ loved first.
Before you could clean yourself up.
Before you could repair your reputation.
Before you could promise never to fail again.
At Calvary, love was not a slogan.
And the risen Christ still calls sinners out of hiding.
So perhaps the most important thing a husband can do tonight is not send this article to his wife and say:
“Look how much I agree with this.”
Perhaps he should put the phone down.
Look into the eyes he once promised to cherish.
“Have I been loving you in a way that makes you feel cherished, safe, heard, and valued—and where have I failed?”
And if the Holy Spirit exposes something...
Because your wife does not need another inspirational quote from a husband unwilling to change.
She needs the fruit of repentance.
And husband, if you are already loving faithfully, quietly, sacrificially...
Not because your wife is flawless.
But because marriage can become one of the places where the Gospel trains us to stop worshiping ourselves.
Maybe you know a husband who desperately needs these words but would never search for them.
Not to start a gender war.
Send it privately to someone who needs hope rather than public embarrassment.
Because there may come a night when anger makes you forget what love requires.
If this exposed something in you, don't hide behind religious language.
“Jesus, teach me to love like You.”
Your testimony may become oxygen for someone else's faith.
And not because anyone should give under pressure.
Scripture teaches that Christian generosity is to come willingly from the heart, not through compulsion.

But voluntary financial support can help Gospel Warrior continue reaching people with Scripture-centered content and expanding resources designed to point wounded, wandering, growing, and searching people toward Jesus.
Sometimes it looks like tagging the one person God placed on your heart.
Sometimes it looks like leaving a testimony that reminds another believer that Jesus still restores broken people.
And sometimes it means helping keep biblical truth moving through a digital world desperately hungry for something deeper than another scroll.
And perhaps tonight, somewhere behind a closed bedroom door, a husband will finally whisper:
“I have not loved you the way I should have.”
And perhaps a wife who stopped expecting those words will begin to cry.
Perhaps professional counseling will be needed.
Perhaps trust will take months or years to rebuild.
Grace does not promise an effortless ending.
when Paul tells you to love your wife as your own body, don't reduce those words to something suitable for a wedding card.
Let them drive you to Christ.
When you're wounded, bring it to Jesus.
When marriage becomes difficult, remember the Cross.
When you forget what love looks like...
Because the deepest miracle is not that two imperfect people somehow build a perfect marriage.
The miracle is that two sinners can continually be brought back beneath the mercy of a perfect Savior.
And maybe the marriage you thought had reached its final chapter is standing one surrendered heart away from a sentence you never expected God to write.
The scar may remain—but in the hands of Jesus, even a scar can become evidence that the wound did not get the final word.
